meta_desc: Class 5 maths How Many Squares made simple: find area and perimeter by counting unit squares, with worked case studies and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: NCERT Chapter 3 hands a child squared paper and asks them to count. Here is how ‘How Many Squares?’ teaches area and perimeter without a single scary formula — plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Class 5 student a sheet of squared paper and ask them to draw a rectangle 5 squares long and 3 squares wide, then count the little squares inside. They land on 15 — and without touching a formula, they have found the area. That one activity is the whole idea behind NCERT Class 5 maths How Many Squares (Chapter 3): you measure how much flat space a shape covers by counting the unit squares that fit inside it, and you measure the boundary by walking around the edge.

What I like about this chapter is that it refuses to start with length × breadth. It makes children see area first. The formula comes later, and by then it feels obvious instead of magic. Here is how to work through it at home.

What Chapter 3 ‘How Many Squares?’ is really about

The chapter builds three ideas, in this order:

  • Area — the number of unit squares that cover a shape. On the NCERT grid, one small square is 1 square centimetre (1 cm²).
  • Perimeter — the total distance around the edge of the shape, found by counting the sides of the squares along the boundary.
  • The surprise — two shapes can have the same area but a different perimeter. This is the part children remember.

Notice that area is measured in squares and perimeter is measured in straight lengths. Mixing up the two is the single most common Class 5 mistake, so it is worth naming out loud early.

Finding area by counting unit squares

For a neat rectangle, counting is easy: rows × columns. A shape that is 4 squares across and 6 down covers 24 squares, so its area is 24 cm². Children quickly spot the shortcut — that is exactly where length × breadth is born, and it lands far better when they discover it than when they are handed it.

The half-square rule for wobbly shapes

The clever bit of this chapter is measuring the area of a leaf, a footprint, or a spilled-ink blob traced on the grid. The rule NCERT uses is simple and honest: count a square as one if more than half of it is inside the shape, and ignore it if less than half is covered. Half-squares are paired up where you can. The answer is an estimate, not an exact figure — and telling a child that estimates are allowed in real measurement is a genuinely useful lesson.

Perimeter: the distance around

Perimeter trips children up because they try to count squares again. It is not about the inside — it is about the fence around the outside. On squared paper you count the unit lengths along the boundary, one edge at a time. For an L-shaped figure you have to go in and out around the corner, and that is exactly what makes L-shapes a favourite in exams.

Same area, different perimeter

Here is the idea that makes Chapter 3 worth its salt. Take 12 unit squares. Arrange them as a 3 × 4 rectangle and the perimeter is 14 cm. Arrange the same 12 squares as a long 2 × 6 rectangle and the perimeter jumps to 16 cm. Same area, different fence. A long, thin shape needs more boundary than a chunky one.

Arrangement of 12 squaresAreaPerimeter
3 × 4 rectangle12 cm²14 cm
2 × 6 rectangle12 cm²16 cm
1 × 12 strip12 cm²26 cm

Ask your child which shape a farmer should choose if fencing is expensive. The chunky 3 × 4 plot needs the least fence for the same land. That is not a trick question — it is real, and it is the counter-intuitive nugget that sticks.

Case study 1: tiling a kitchen floor

NCERT frames area through everyday scenes, and this is the kind of passage the case-study practice uses.

Meera’s kitchen floor is a rectangle 5 tiles long and 4 tiles wide. Each square tile costs ₹30.

  • How many tiles cover the floor? Count the grid: 5 × 4 = 20 tiles. The area is 20 tile-squares.
  • What is the total cost? 20 × ₹30 = ₹600.
  • If the floor were 10 long and 2 wide instead, would the number of tiles change? No — 10 × 2 is still 20 tiles, same area. But the room’s perimeter, and so the skirting needed along the walls, would be larger.

That last question is the whole chapter in one line: area can stay fixed while perimeter changes.

Case study 2: measuring a mango leaf

Ravi traces a mango leaf on 1 cm squared paper. He counts 18 squares fully inside the outline and 8 squares that are more than half covered.

Using the half-square rule, both the full squares and the more-than-half squares count as one each: 18 + 8 = 26. So the leaf’s area is about 26 cm². If Ravi’s friend counts 27, that is fine — measuring a curved leaf on a grid always gives an estimate, and answers within a square or two are all correct. Teaching a child to say ‘about 26’ rather than pretending to an exact number is the honest habit this chapter rewards.

A quick word on common slip-ups

In my experience with Class 5, three errors show up again and again: counting inside squares when perimeter was asked, forgetting the units (cm for perimeter, cm² for area), and rounding half-squares the wrong way. Fix those three and most of the chapter takes care of itself.

Try the quiz, then the case-study practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering exactly what Chapter 3 asks — counting squares for area, the half-square rule, perimeter, and the same-area-different-perimeter idea. Let your child attempt it, then read the explanations together. quiz.title: Class 5 How Many Squares? Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on area, perimeter and counting unit squares from NCERT Chapter 3. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 5 area and perimeter by counting squares

questions.q: A rectangle is 6 squares long and 3 squares wide. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area is rows times columns: 6 times 3 = 18 unit squares, so 18 cm squared.

questions.q: One small square on the NCERT grid stands for an area of:
questions.explanation: Each unit square on the grid is 1 centimetre by 1 centimetre, so its area is 1 cm squared.

questions.q: What is the perimeter of a square that is 4 units on each side?
questions.explanation: Perimeter is the distance around: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 units.

questions.q: When measuring a leaf on squared paper, you count a square if:
questions.explanation: The half-square rule counts a square as one only when more than half of it lies inside the shape.

questions.q: A 3 by 4 rectangle and a 2 by 6 rectangle both have area 12 squares. What about their perimeters?
options: The 3 by 4 has a smaller perimeter
The 2 by 6 has a smaller perimeter
questions.explanation: The chunkier 3 by 4 has perimeter 14, while the longer 2 by 6 has perimeter 16. Same area, different perimeter.

questions.q: A floor is 5 tiles long and 4 tiles wide. How many tiles cover it?
questions.explanation: Count the grid: 5 times 4 = 20 tiles, so the area is 20 tile-squares.

questions.q: Perimeter is measured in which kind of unit?
questions.explanation: Perimeter is a length around the edge, so it is measured in centimetres. Area uses square centimetres.

questions.q: Ravi counts 14 full squares and 6 more-than-half squares under a leaf. About what is its area?
questions.explanation: Full squares plus more-than-half squares each count as one: 14 + 6 = about 20 cm squared.

faq.q: What is NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 3 about?
faq.a: Chapter 3, ‘How Many Squares?’, teaches area and perimeter by counting unit squares on a grid instead of jumping straight to formulas. Children measure how many squares cover a shape (area) and how far it is around the edge (perimeter).

faq.q: How do you find the area of a shape by counting squares?
faq.a: Place the shape on squared paper and count the unit squares inside it. For a rectangle it is simply rows × columns. For a wobbly shape like a leaf, count a square only when more than half of it is covered, which gives a good estimate.

faq.q: Can two shapes have the same area but different perimeter?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the key idea of the chapter. Twelve squares made into a 3 × 4 rectangle have a perimeter of 14 cm, but the same twelve as a 2 × 6 rectangle have a perimeter of 16 cm. A long, thin shape needs more boundary than a chunky one.

faq.q: What is the difference between area and perimeter for Class 5?
faq.a: Area is the flat space a shape covers, counted in square units like cm². Perimeter is the distance all the way around the edge, measured in length units like cm. Confusing the two is the most common mistake in this chapter.
